docs.expected: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: very low storage cost, expedited retrieval in 1–5 minutes. Triggers: "infrequently accessed archives", "retrievable within minutes", "a few times a year", "MOST cost-effective".
docs.why_not: Standard and Standard-IA cost more for rarely used data; One Zone-IA is a single AZ, not for long-term archives.

question.stem: A company stores 500 TB of infrequently accessed log archives that must be retrievable within minutes a few times a year. Which S3 storage class is MOST cost-effective?
question.explanation: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers very low storage cost for rarely accessed archives, with expedited retrievals available in minutes, fitting the access pattern. S3 Standard and Standard-IA cost more for rarely accessed data. One Zone-IA stores in a single AZ and is not suited for durable long-term archives.

docs.concept: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: unpredictable access pattern
docs.tests: Choosing a storage class for millions of objects with unpredictable access and no manual tiering.
docs.expected: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on usage, with no retrieval fees or performance impact. Triggers: "unpredictable access patterns", "without manual tiering", "no performance impact".
docs.why_not: Standard doesn't optimize cost; Deep Archive has slow retrieval; One Zone-IA reduces resilience.

question.stem: An application has unpredictable access patterns across millions of S3 objects, and the team wants to minimize cost without performance impact or manual tiering. Which storage class is BEST?
question.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage, optimizing cost for unpredictable patterns with no retrieval fees for frequent/infrequent tiers and no performance impact. Standard does not optimize cost. Deep Archive has long retrieval times. One Zone-IA reduces durability.

docs.concept: EC2 purchasing: Compute Savings Plans — discount with family flexibility
docs.tests: Choosing a purchase model for a steady 24/7 load over 3 years with the ability to change instance family.
docs.expected: 3-year Compute Savings Plan: deep discount that applies to any family, size, Region, plus Fargate/Lambda. Triggers: "steady 24/7 baseline", "three years", "flexibility to change instance family".
docs.why_not: On-Demand is the most expensive for a constant load; Spot is for interruptible jobs; a Standard RI is tied to an instance family.

question.stem: A team wants to reduce EC2 costs for a steady 24/7 baseline workload running for the next three years, with flexibility to change instance family within a compute type. Which purchasing option is BEST?
options: Standard Reserved Instances locked to one instance type
question.explanation: A 3-year Compute Savings Plan offers deep discounts for steady usage and applies flexibly across instance families, sizes, Regions, and even Fargate/Lambda. On-Demand is most expensive for steady use. Spot is for interruptible work. Standard RIs give discounts but lock to a specific instance family, reducing flexibility.

docs.concept: Cost Explorer + Budgets: cost-driver analysis and threshold alerts
docs.tests: Which tools show which services/accounts drive cost growth and alert when thresholds are exceeded.
docs.expected: AWS Cost Explorer analyzes spending trends by service and account; AWS Budgets alerts when a threshold is exceeded. Triggers: "which services and accounts are driving cost", "alerts when spending exceeds thresholds", (Choose two).
docs.why_not: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries logs; Config tracks resource configuration; neither analyzes cost.

question.stem: A company wants to identify which AWS services and accounts are driving cost increases and to set alerts when spending exceeds thresholds. Which tools should they use? (Choose two)
question.explanation: Cost Explorer visualizes and analyzes spending trends by service and account, and AWS Budgets triggers alerts when costs exceed defined thresholds. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries logs and Config tracks resource configuration; neither provides cost alerting or trend analysis.

docs.concept: Athena: serverless SQL over data in S3
docs.tests: Choosing a service for ad hoc serverless SQL queries over an S3 data lake with pay-per-query pricing.
docs.expected: Amazon Athena: serverless, SQL directly on S3, pay per data scanned. Triggers: "ad hoc SQL", "directly on S3", "without provisioning servers", "pay per query".
docs.why_not: Redshift provisioned and EMR mean managing and paying for running clusters; RDS is OLTP, not queries over S3 files.

question.stem: A data lake stores files in S3, and analysts want to run ad hoc SQL queries directly on the data without provisioning servers, paying only per query. Which service fits?
question.explanation: Athena is a serverless query service that runs SQL directly on S3 data and charges per amount of data scanned, ideal for ad hoc queries with no infrastructure. A Redshift provisioned cluster and EMR require managing and paying for running clusters. RDS is for transactional databases, not querying S3 files.

docs.concept: EC2 purchasing: Spot for interruptible, fault-tolerant batch jobs
docs.tests: Cheapest compute option for a nightly ETL that can be rerun if interrupted.
docs.expected: Spot Instances: maximum discount for interruptible, restartable batch jobs. Triggers: "nightly", "about two hours", "tolerate occasional reruns", "minimize compute cost".
docs.why_not: On-Demand costs more; Reserved Instances are for steady 24/7 load, not 2 hours a day; Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive, for licensing/compliance.

question.stem: A company runs nightly EC2-based ETL that takes about two hours. They want to minimize compute cost and can tolerate occasional reruns if interrupted. Which option is MOST cost-effective?
question.explanation: Spot Instances provide the deepest discounts and suit interruptible, restartable batch jobs like nightly ETL, minimizing cost. On-Demand is more expensive. Reserved Instances suit steady 24/7 usage, not occasional nightly runs. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option, used for licensing or compliance.

docs.concept: S3 Lifecycle: transition and expiration by object age
docs.tests: Simplest way to automatically move objects to a cheaper class after 30 days and delete them after 365.
docs.expected: S3 Lifecycle policy with a transition rule (30 days → cheaper class) and an expiration rule (365 days), no code. Triggers: "transition after 30 days", "deleted after 365 days", "automatically", "simplest".
docs.why_not: A scheduled Lambda is unnecessary custom code; S3 Replication copies rather than changing class; manual moves mean errors and overhead.

question.stem: An S3 bucket holds data that should transition to cheaper storage after 30 days and be deleted after 365 days automatically. What is the simplest way to implement this?
options: Write a Lambda function on a schedule to move and delete objects
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy with transition and expiration rules
question.explanation: An S3 Lifecycle policy automates transitions to cheaper classes after a set age and expires objects after a defined period with no code. A scheduled Lambda is unnecessary custom work. Replication copies data rather than tiering it, and manual moves are error-prone and high overhead.

docs.concept: Snow Family: offline transfer of hundreds of TB over a thin link
docs.tests: Choosing how to move petabyte-scale data when network transfer would take months.
docs.expected: AWS Snowball / Snow Family: physical devices for encrypted offline transfer of petabytes. Triggers: "10 PB", "network would take months", "physical bulk transfer appliance".
docs.why_not: DataSync and direct S3 upload are limited by network bandwidth; Storage Gateway is hybrid access, not a one-time 10 PB migration.

question.stem: A company transfers 10 PB of data to AWS, and their network would take months. They need a secure, physical bulk transfer appliance. Which service is appropriate?
options: Direct upload to S3 over the public internet
question.explanation: The AWS Snow Family ships physical devices for petabyte-scale offline data transfer when network transfer is impractical, with encryption in transit. DataSync and direct uploads depend on network bandwidth and would take too long. Storage Gateway provides hybrid storage access, not bulk one-time migration of 10 PB.

docs.concept: EBS io2: Provisioned IOPS for latency-sensitive databases
docs.tests: Choosing an EBS type for a transactional DB with consistently high IOPS and low latency.
docs.expected: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 / io2 Block Express): guaranteed high IOPS and low latency. Triggers: "consistent high IOPS", "latency-sensitive transactional workload", database.
docs.why_not: gp2 is baseline with burst, no guarantee of sustained high IOPS; st1/sc1 are HDD for throughput/cold data, not low-latency I/O.

question.stem: An EBS-backed database needs consistent high IOPS performance for a latency-sensitive transactional workload. Which EBS volume type should be used?
options: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 or io2 Block Express)
question.explanation: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2/io2 Block Express) delivers consistent, high IOPS and low latency for demanding transactional databases. gp2 offers baseline burstable performance not guaranteed for sustained high IOPS. st1 and sc1 are HDD types optimized for throughput or cold storage, unsuitable for low-latency transactional I/O.

docs.concept: CloudFront: edge caching and compression to cut data transfer out
docs.tests: Which two changes cut data transfer cost and latency for repeated requests to the origin.
docs.expected: CloudFront caches content at the edge (less origin load and data transfer out) + compresses text responses at the edge (fewer bytes). Triggers: "reduce data transfer costs", "repeated requests to origin", "global users", (Choose two).
docs.why_not: Serving everything from EC2 in one Region raises cost and latency; a bigger instance doesn't cut transfer cost.

question.stem: A company wants to reduce data transfer costs and latency for repeated requests to its origin while serving global users. Which two changes help achieve this? (Choose two)
options: Enable compression for text-based responses at the edge
Use Amazon CloudFront to cache content at the edge
Serve all content directly from EC2 in one Region
question.explanation: CloudFront caches content at edge locations to cut origin load and data-transfer-out costs and lower latency, while edge compression reduces the bytes transferred for text responses. Serving from one Region raises transfer cost and latency for distant users. A larger instance does not reduce data transfer cost.

docs.concept: Fargate: serverless containers with no instance management
docs.tests: Choosing a launch type for containers with no EC2 capacity management, paying for task vCPU and memory.
docs.expected: AWS Fargate: serverless container execution, pay only for requested vCPU and memory. Triggers: "eliminate EC2 capacity management", "pay only for vCPU and memory their tasks consume".
docs.why_not: ECS EC2 launch type and self-managed Kubernetes require managing instances; Reserved Instances are an EC2 pricing model, not serverless.

question.stem: A team running containers wants to eliminate EC2 capacity management and pay only for the vCPU and memory their tasks consume. Which launch type should they choose?
options: Amazon ECS on EC2 launch type
question.explanation: AWS Fargate runs containers serverlessly, removing EC2 capacity management and charging only for the vCPU and memory requested by tasks. The ECS EC2 launch type and self-managed Kubernetes still require managing instances. Reserved Instances are an EC2 pricing model, not a serverless container option.

docs.concept: Redshift: columnar DWH + Spectrum for querying S3
docs.tests: Choosing a petabyte-scale analytics warehouse with columnar storage and queries over S3.
docs.expected: Amazon Redshift (columnar DWH for complex SQL aggregations) + Redshift Spectrum (queries data in S3 without loading). Triggers: "petabyte-scale analytics warehouse", "complex SQL aggregations", "columnar", "query S3 data directly".
docs.why_not: DynamoDB is NoSQL key-value; RDS for MySQL is row-based OLTP; ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

question.stem: A petabyte-scale analytics warehouse must run complex SQL aggregations across structured data with columnar storage and the ability to query S3 data directly. Which service fits?
question.explanation: Redshift is a columnar data warehouse built for large-scale analytical SQL, and Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 without loading it. DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store. RDS for MySQL is row-based OLTP, not optimized for petabyte analytics. ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

docs.concept: VPC endpoints: S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints instead of NAT (savings)
docs.tests: How to cut NAT Gateway data processing charges for EC2 traffic to S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region.
docs.expected: Create Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB: a private route with no per-GB charge, traffic bypasses the NAT Gateway. Triggers: "NAT Gateway data processing charges", "S3 and DynamoDB", "same Region", "MOST cost-effective".
docs.why_not: More NAT Gateways cost more; IGW and public subnets expose instances and don't solve it privately.

question.stem: A company wants to reduce NAT Gateway data processing charges for EC2 instances that frequently access S3 and DynamoDB within the same Region. What is the MOST cost-effective change?
options: Create S3 and DynamoDB Gateway VPC endpoints
question.explanation: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route traffic privately within AWS at no per-GB cost, bypassing the NAT Gateway and avoiding its data processing charges. Adding NAT Gateways increases cost. Internet Gateways and public subnets expose instances and still incur transfer costs for these services via NAT otherwise.

docs.concept: Compute Optimizer: rightsizing by actual utilization
docs.tests: Which service gives rightsizing recommendations for underutilized EC2.
docs.expected: AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization metrics and recommends optimal instance types/sizes. Triggers: "idle and underutilized", "recommendations to right-size", "reduce cost".
docs.why_not: Inspector is vulnerabilities; Config is configuration state; CloudWatch alarms alert but don't recommend sizes.

question.stem: A company has many idle and underutilized EC2 instances and wants recommendations to right-size them to reduce cost. Which service provides this analysis?
question.explanation: AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization metrics and recommends optimal instance types and sizes to reduce cost and improve performance. Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, Config tracks configuration state, and CloudWatch alarms alert on metrics but do not recommend right-sizing.

docs.concept: FSx for Windows File Server: SMB/NTFS with Active Directory integration
docs.tests: Choosing a managed file system for a Windows app with SMB, NTFS and AD.
docs.expected: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: Windows-native, SMB, NTFS, Active Directory integration. Triggers: "Windows-based", "SMB", "NTFS", "Active Directory integration".
docs.why_not: EFS is NFS for Linux; S3 is object storage with no SMB; FSx for Lustre is HPC, not Windows file shares.

question.stem: A Windows-based application requires a fully managed, high-performance shared file system supporting SMB and NTFS with Active Directory integration. Which service is correct?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
question.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed Windows-native file system with SMB, NTFS, and Active Directory integration. EFS is NFS for Linux. S3 is object storage without SMB. FSx for Lustre targets high-performance computing workloads, not Windows file shares.

docs.concept: DMS: DB migration with CDC and minimal downtime
docs.tests: Choosing a service to migrate a production DB with continuous change replication until cutover.
docs.expected: AWS DMS with ongoing replication: full load + CDC, near-zero-downtime cutover. Triggers: "minimal downtime", "continuously replicating changes until cutover".
docs.why_not: Snowball is offline bulk transfer, not live replication; Transfer Acceleration speeds up S3 uploads; mysqldump/import requires long downtime.

question.stem: A company wants to migrate a production database to AWS with minimal downtime, continuously replicating changes until cutover. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with ongoing replication
question.explanation: DMS performs an initial load and then continuously replicates ongoing changes (CDC), enabling near-zero-downtime cutover. Snowball is for bulk offline transfer, not live replication. Transfer Acceleration speeds S3 uploads, and a manual dump/import requires extended downtime during the migration window.

docs.concept: CloudWatch alarms: alert on a metric threshold (CPUUtilization)
docs.tests: Which service automatically alerts when average EC2 CPU stays above 80% for 5 minutes.
docs.expected: Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric (threshold 80%, period 5 min) → SNS notification or action. Triggers: "alerted automatically", "CPU utilization exceeds 80% for five minutes".
docs.why_not: CloudTrail is API calls, not metrics; Config is configuration compliance; X-Ray is request tracing.

question.stem: An operations team must be alerted automatically when average EC2 CPU utilization exceeds 80% for five minutes. Which AWS service provides this monitoring and alerting?
question.explanation: CloudWatch alarms evaluate metrics like CPUUtilization against thresholds over a period and trigger notifications or actions, meeting the requirement. CloudTrail records API calls, not performance metrics. Config tracks configuration compliance, and X-Ray traces application requests, not infrastructure metrics.

docs.concept: CloudWatch agent + Logs Insights: centralized logs and queries
docs.tests: How to centralize logs from many EC2 instances and query them for troubleshooting with minimal overhead.
docs.expected: Install the CloudWatch agent → ship logs to CloudWatch Logs → query interactively with Logs Insights. Triggers: "centralize logs from many EC2", "run queries to troubleshoot", "LEAST operational overhead".
docs.why_not: Manual copying to S3 and email is overhead and slow; logs kept only on instances are lost when they're replaced.

question.stem: A team wants to centralize logs from many EC2 instances and run queries to troubleshoot issues. Which combination achieves this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Store logs only on each instance
Install the CloudWatch agent to ship logs to CloudWatch Logs and query with Logs Insights
Copy log files to S3 manually each day
question.explanation: The CloudWatch agent streams instance logs to CloudWatch Logs, and Logs Insights provides fast interactive querying, centralizing troubleshooting with little management. Manual S3 copies and emailing logs are high overhead and slow. Keeping logs only on instances loses them when instances are replaced.

docs.concept: AWS Config: configuration history and continuous compliance
docs.tests: Which service records the full history of resource configuration changes and evaluates them against rules.
docs.expected: AWS Config: configuration history + continuous evaluation against Config rules. Triggers: "complete history of configuration changes", "evaluate against compliance rules over time".
docs.why_not: CloudTrail is API activity, not configuration state over time; CloudWatch is metrics and logs; Trusted Advisor is point-in-time best-practice checks.

question.stem: A company must record a complete history of configuration changes to all AWS resources and evaluate them against compliance rules over time. Which service should they enable?
question.explanation: AWS Config records resource configuration history and continuously evaluates resources against rules for compliance. CloudTrail logs API activity but not full configuration state over time. CloudWatch monitors metrics and logs. Trusted Advisor gives point-in-time best-practice checks, not configuration history.

docs.concept: CloudFormation: infrastructure as code for repeatable environments
docs.tests: Choosing a native service for reproducible infrastructure provisioning from versioned templates.
docs.expected: AWS CloudFormation: IaC templates under version control, repeatable deployment across environments. Triggers: "identical, repeatable infrastructure", "multiple environments", "version-controlled templates", "AWS natively".
docs.why_not: The console and ad hoc CLI aren't repeatable or tracked; SSM Run Command runs commands on instances but doesn't manage stacks.

question.stem: A team wants to provision identical, repeatable infrastructure across multiple environments using version-controlled templates managed by AWS natively. Which service is BEST?
options: Editing resources with the CLI ad hoc
Manually creating resources in the console
question.explanation: CloudFormation defines infrastructure as code in templates that can be version-controlled and deployed repeatably across environments. Console and ad hoc CLI changes are not repeatable or tracked. Run Command executes operational commands on instances but does not provision and manage full infrastructure stacks.

docs.concept: X-Ray: distributed tracing to find latency in microservices
docs.tests: Which service provides end-to-end request tracing across microservices.
docs.expected: AWS X-Ray traces requests across distributed services, with a service map and latency analysis. Triggers: "trace requests across microservices", "find bottlenecks", "end-to-end tracing".
docs.why_not: CloudWatch Logs stores logs; CloudTrail is API calls; Config is configuration; none provide request traces.

question.stem: An application's distributed requests are slow, and the team needs to trace requests across microservices to find bottlenecks. Which service provides end-to-end tracing?
question.explanation: AWS X-Ray traces requests as they flow through distributed microservices, producing service maps and latency analysis to pinpoint bottlenecks. CloudWatch Logs stores log data, CloudTrail records API calls, and Config tracks configuration; none provide distributed request tracing.

docs.concept: Systems Manager Patch Manager: scheduled fleet patching without SSH
docs.tests: How to patch the OS of hundreds of EC2 instances on a schedule and get a compliance report without SSH.
docs.expected: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager: scheduled patching (maintenance windows, patch baselines) via the SSM agent plus patch compliance reporting. Triggers: "patch operating systems", "hundreds of instances", "on a schedule", "report compliance", "without SSH".
docs.why_not: Inspector finds vulnerabilities but doesn't patch; CloudFormation is provisioning; manual SSH scripts mean overhead and errors.

question.stem: A company wants to patch operating systems on hundreds of EC2 instances on a schedule and report compliance, without SSH access to each host. Which service should they use?
question.explanation: Systems Manager Patch Manager automates patching on a schedule and reports patch compliance across fleets via the SSM agent, avoiding per-host SSH. Inspector scans for vulnerabilities but does not apply patches. CloudFormation provisions infrastructure. Manual SSH scripts are high overhead and error-prone.

docs.concept: Auto Scaling: self-healing via health checks and desired capacity
docs.tests: Which configuration automatically replaces an EC2 instance that fails its health check.
docs.expected: Auto Scaling group with health checks (EC2/ELB) terminates an unhealthy instance and launches a replacement on its own. Triggers: "failing its health check", "replacing it without human intervention", "self-healing".
docs.why_not: A dashboard only visualizes; manual monitoring isn't automatic; termination protection gets in the way of replacement.

question.stem: A team needs to automatically respond to an EC2 instance failing its health check by replacing it without human intervention. Which configuration provides this self-healing?
options: An Auto Scaling group with health checks that terminates and replaces unhealthy instances
question.explanation: An Auto Scaling group monitors instance health and automatically terminates and launches replacements for unhealthy instances, providing self-healing. A dashboard only visualizes metrics. Manual monitoring is not automatic. Termination protection actually prevents instances from being terminated, blocking replacement.

docs.concept: EventBridge: content-based event routing to multiple targets
docs.tests: Choosing a service to route events from many AWS services to different targets by content.
docs.expected: Amazon EventBridge: event bus with rules, content-based filtering and many targets. Triggers: "routed to different targets based on the content of events", "many AWS services", "flexible filtering rules".
docs.why_not: SQS only queues, with no rule-based routing; CloudTrail records API calls; CloudWatch dashboards are visualization.

question.stem: A company wants notifications routed to different targets based on the content of events from many AWS services, with flexible filtering rules. Which service is BEST?
question.explanation: EventBridge ingests events from AWS services and custom sources, applies content-based filtering rules, and routes matching events to many targets. SQS only queues messages without rule-based routing. CloudTrail records API activity, and CloudWatch dashboards visualize metrics rather than route events.

docs.concept: Deployment: blue/green for minimal risk and fast rollback
docs.tests: Choosing a deployment strategy where the old version keeps running until the new one is verified.
docs.expected: Blue/green deployment: the new version (green) runs alongside the old one (blue), traffic switches after verification, fast rollback. Triggers: "keeping the previous version running until the new one is verified", "minimizing risk".
docs.why_not: Updating everything in place at once risks a full outage; stopping instances or recreating the ASG causes downtime.

question.stem: An operations team wants to deploy application updates to an Auto Scaling group while keeping the previous version running until the new one is verified, minimizing risk. Which deployment strategy is BEST?
options: Deleting the Auto Scaling group and recreating it
Manually stopping all instances during deployment
In-place update of all instances at once
question.explanation: A blue/green deployment runs the new version alongside the old and shifts traffic only after verification, enabling quick rollback and minimal risk. Updating all instances at once risks a full outage if the release is faulty. Stopping instances or recreating the group causes downtime.

docs.concept: CloudWatch Anomaly Detection: ML alerts without static thresholds
docs.tests: Which CloudWatch feature automatically finds anomalies in metrics without manual thresholds.
docs.expected: CloudWatch Anomaly Detection: ML learns the metric's normal pattern (band) and alerts on deviations. Triggers: "detect anomalies in metrics automatically", "without manually setting static thresholds".
docs.why_not: Static threshold alarms need manual thresholds; CloudTrail Insights is API-activity anomalies, not metrics; Config rules are compliance.

question.stem: A company needs operational visibility and wants to detect anomalies in metrics automatically without manually setting static thresholds. Which CloudWatch capability helps?
question.explanation: CloudWatch Anomaly Detection applies machine learning to learn normal metric patterns and alert on deviations without manual static thresholds. Static threshold alarms require manually chosen limits. CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity, not metric anomalies, and Config rules evaluate configuration compliance.

docs.concept: SSM Automation runbooks + CloudWatch alarm actions: auto-remediation
docs.tests: How to automate an operational response (service restart) via a runbook when a CloudWatch alarm fires.
docs.expected: Systems Manager Automation runbooks (repeatable remediation steps) + CloudWatch alarm actions that invoke SSM Automation or Lambda. Triggers: "automate operational responses", "when alarm fires", "predefined runbooks", (Choose two).
docs.why_not: Macie classifies sensitive data and Shield protects against DDoS; neither relates to remediation automation.

question.stem: A team wants to automate operational responses, such as restarting a service when a CloudWatch alarm fires, using predefined runbooks. Which service provides this automation? (Choose two)
options: Amazon CloudWatch alarm actions invoking SSM or Lambda
question.explanation: Systems Manager Automation runbooks define repeatable remediation steps, and CloudWatch alarm actions can invoke SSM Automation or Lambda to trigger them automatically. Macie classifies sensitive data and Shield mitigates DDoS; neither automates operational remediation.

docs.concept: S3 Object Lock: compliance mode (WORM, not even root can delete)
docs.tests: How to store CloudTrail logs immutably for 7 years, preventing deletion and modification.
docs.expected: S3 bucket with Object Lock in Compliance mode and a retention period: WORM, nobody (not even root) can delete/modify until it expires. Triggers: "immutably", "seven years", "preventing deletion or modification", compliance.
docs.why_not: EBS isn't immutable and is tied to an instance; CloudWatch Logs with 30-day retention doesn't cover 7 years; DynamoDB isn't for immutable log archives.

question.stem: A company must store CloudTrail logs immutably for seven years to meet compliance, preventing deletion or modification. Which configuration is BEST?
options: Store logs in an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode and a retention period
Store logs on an EBS volume
Keep logs only in CloudWatch Logs with a 30-day retention
question.explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces write-once-read-many retention so logs cannot be deleted or altered, even by root, for the specified period. EBS volumes are not immutable and tie to instances. A 30-day CloudWatch retention fails the seven-year requirement, and DynamoDB is not designed for immutable log archives.

docs.concept: IAM: cross-account role for a third party with External ID
docs.tests: How to securely give a third-party vendor (another AWS account) access to S3 so that only the intended account can assume the role.
docs.expected: IAM role with a trust policy whose principal is the vendor's account, + an sts:ExternalId condition (confused deputy protection). Triggers: "third-party vendor", "assume the role from their own account", "MOST secure".
docs.why_not: IAM user access keys sent by email are long-lived secrets; a public bucket exposes data to everyone; ACLs can't control assume role for cross-account IAM users.

question.stem: A company needs to grant a third-party SaaS vendor's AWS account read-only access to objects in a specific S3 bucket. The vendor will assume the role from their own account. What is the MOST secure way to enforce that only the intended vendor account can assume the role?
options: Create an IAM role with a trust policy specifying the vendor's account as principal and add an external ID condition
Add the vendor's IAM user ARN to the bucket ACL
Make the bucket public and share the URL with the vendor
Create an IAM user with access keys and email them to the vendor
question.explanation: A cross-account IAM role with a trust policy naming the vendor account plus an sts:ExternalId condition prevents the confused-deputy problem and is the recommended pattern for third-party access. IAM user keys are long-lived and risky to email. A public bucket exposes data to everyone, and ACLs cannot reference cross-account IAM users this way for fine-grained role assumption.

docs.concept: S3 encryption: enforce SSE-KMS via default encryption + bucket policy
docs.tests: How to guarantee every object is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key and reject uploads without SSE.
docs.expected: Default encryption SSE-KMS with a CMK + bucket policy Deny s3:PutObject when the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is missing/wrong. Triggers: "customer managed KMS key", "upload without encryption is rejected".
docs.why_not: SSE-S3 doesn't use a customer managed key; versioning doesn't encrypt; a Lambda that deletes objects after upload leaves a window of unencrypted storage.

question.stem: A security team wants to ensure that all data stored in an S3 bucket is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and that any upload without server-side encryption is rejected. What should they configure?
options: Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS using the CMK and add a bucket policy denying PutObject requests lacking the correct encryption header
Use a Lambda function to delete unencrypted objects after upload
Enable S3 default encryption with SSE-S3 only
question.explanation: Default encryption with SSE-KMS ensures objects are encrypted at rest with the CMK, and a bucket policy that denies PutObject when the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is missing or incorrect enforces it at upload time. SSE-S3 does not use a customer managed key. Versioning does not enforce encryption, and deleting after upload still allows a window of unencrypted storage.

docs.concept: SCP: deny disabling CloudTrail in all Organizations accounts
docs.tests: Which mechanism denies actions in member accounts regardless of their own IAM permissions.
docs.expected: SCP on the OU with Deny cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail — caps maximum permissions, overrides local IAM permissions. Triggers: "AWS Organizations", "regardless of the account's own IAM permissions", "prevent any member account".
docs.why_not: Permission boundaries are per principal, easy to miss; an IAM role with a deny doesn't cover everyone; a CloudWatch alarm only reacts after the fact, doesn't prevent.

question.stem: An organization uses AWS Organizations and wants to prevent any member account from disabling CloudTrail, regardless of the account's own IAM permissions. What should they use?
options: A CloudWatch alarm that re-enables CloudTrail
IAM permission boundaries on each account
An IAM role with deny statements
A Service Control Policy (SCP) attached to the organizational unit denying cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
question.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for accounts in an OU and can deny CloudTrail-disabling actions across the entire organization, overriding local IAM grants. Permission boundaries apply per-principal and must be attached individually, which is error-prone. An IAM role and a CloudWatch remediation alarm do not prevent the action from succeeding in the first place.

docs.concept: Secrets Manager: automatic rotation of DB credentials
docs.tests: Choosing a service to store DB credentials with automatic rotation and secure retrieval at runtime.
docs.expected: AWS Secrets Manager with rotation enabled (Lambda rotation, built in for RDS). Triggers: "automatic rotation", "database credentials", "minimal operational overhead".
docs.why_not: Parameter Store standard parameters — no built-in rotation; an encrypted S3 object and KMS data keys — no rotation at all, custom code needed.

question.stem: A company stores database credentials in application code. They want automatic rotation and secure retrieval at runtime with minimal operational overhead. Which service is MOST appropriate?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameters
AWS Secrets Manager with rotation enabled
Storing the credentials in an encrypted S3 object
question.explanation: Secrets Manager natively supports automatic rotation via Lambda and provides secure, audited retrieval, making it ideal for database credentials. Parameter Store standard parameters lack built-in rotation. An encrypted S3 object and KMS data keys provide no rotation mechanism and require custom code.

docs.concept: IAM: role via instance profile instead of access keys on EC2
docs.tests: How to give an app on EC2 access to the S3 API without storing long-term credentials on the instance.
docs.expected: Attach an IAM role via an instance profile — temporary, automatically rotated credentials through the instance metadata service. Triggers: "forbids storing long-term credentials", "EC2 needs to call AWS API".
docs.why_not: Access keys in user data or env vars are long-lived secrets on the host; root credentials — never.

question.stem: A web application running on EC2 instances needs to call the S3 API. The security team forbids storing any long-term credentials on the instances. What is the recommended approach?
options: Embed an IAM user's access keys in the user data script
Attach an IAM role to the instances via an instance profile
Store credentials in environment variables set at boot
question.explanation: Attaching an IAM role through an instance profile delivers temporary, automatically rotated credentials via the instance metadata service, eliminating long-term secrets. Embedding access keys or environment-variable credentials stores long-lived secrets on the host. Using root credentials is never acceptable.

docs.concept: CloudHSM: customer-controlled single-tenant FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSM
docs.tests: Choosing between KMS and CloudHSM when keys must stay in a dedicated HSM fully controlled by the customer.
docs.expected: AWS CloudHSM — single-tenant HSM, FIPS 140-2 Level 3, customer fully manages the keys. Triggers: "FIPS 140-2 Level 3", "hardware boundary that they fully control", "single-tenant".
docs.why_not: KMS (AWS managed and customer managed keys) is multi-tenant, keys are managed by AWS infrastructure; ACM is for TLS certificates, not arbitrary encryption keys.

question.stem: A company must encrypt sensitive data and meet a compliance requirement that the encryption keys never leave a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware boundary that they fully control. Which service meets this need?
options: AWS KMS with AWS managed keys
AWS KMS with customer managed keys
question.explanation: CloudHSM provides single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security modules that the customer fully controls. KMS shared multi-tenant infrastructure (managed or customer keys) is Level 3 for the HSMs but not single-tenant customer-controlled to the same degree, and the keys are managed by AWS infrastructure. ACM manages TLS certificates, not arbitrary encryption keys.

docs.concept: CloudTrail: API call auditing with long-term retention in S3 + Glacier
docs.tests: Which services give a complete log of API calls (who, when, from where) with cheap multi-year retention.
docs.expected: CloudTrail trail → S3 bucket + S3 lifecycle policy → Glacier for older logs. Triggers: "every API call", "identity, time, source IP", "retained for several years", "cost-effectively".
docs.why_not: VPC Flow Logs — network traffic, not API calls; CloudWatch detailed monitoring — metrics; DynamoDB — expensive for a log archive.

question.stem: An auditor needs a record of every API call made in an AWS account, including the identity, time, and source IP, retained for several years. Which combination meets this requirement MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two)
options: Enable CloudWatch detailed monitoring on all resources
Enable a CloudTrail trail delivering logs to an S3 bucket
Apply an S3 lifecycle policy to transition CloudTrail logs to Glacier
Use VPC Flow Logs to capture API activity
question.explanation: A CloudTrail trail records management and data API calls with identity, time, and source IP, and delivering to S3 enables long-term retention. An S3 lifecycle policy transitioning older logs to Glacier minimizes storage cost over years. VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic, not API calls; detailed monitoring is metrics, not audit logs; DynamoDB is unnecessarily expensive for this.

docs.concept: STS: SAML 2.0 federation (AssumeRoleWithSAML)
docs.tests: Which service issues temporary credentials to users authenticated by a corporate SAML IdP.
docs.expected: AWS STS via SAML federation — AssumeRoleWithSAML. Triggers: "temporary credentials", "corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider".
docs.why_not: Cognito user pools — for application end users; Identity Center is an option, but STS still issues the credentials; Directory Service — a managed directory, not a credential broker.

question.stem: A developer needs temporary AWS credentials for users authenticating through a corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider. Which service issues these credentials?
question.explanation: AWS STS supports SAML 2.0 federation through AssumeRoleWithSAML, issuing temporary credentials to users authenticated by a corporate IdP. Cognito user pools target application end users, not corporate SAML federation into AWS. Identity Center is one option but the underlying credential issuance is STS, and Directory Service is a managed directory, not a credential broker for SAML.

docs.concept: Security Hub: aggregate and prioritize security findings across accounts
docs.tests: Which service continuously aggregates and prioritizes findings (public buckets, overly permissive IAM policies) across all accounts.
docs.expected: AWS Security Hub integrated with GuardDuty, Config, IAM Access Analyzer — a single prioritized view of security posture. Triggers: "across all accounts", "continuously", "findings prioritized".
docs.why_not: Config alone records configuration but doesn't aggregate/prioritize cross-service findings; Macie — sensitive data in S3; Trusted Advisor — limited checks.

question.stem: A company wants to detect publicly accessible S3 buckets and overly permissive IAM policies across all accounts continuously, with findings prioritized. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Security Hub with GuardDuty and Config integrated
question.explanation: Security Hub aggregates and prioritizes findings from integrated services like Config, IAM Access Analyzer, and GuardDuty across accounts, providing continuous posture management. Config alone records configuration but does not prioritize cross-service findings. Macie focuses on sensitive data discovery in S3. Trusted Advisor offers limited checks without the same continuous, multi-account prioritization.

docs.concept: S3 encryption: client-side — AWS never sees plaintext or keys
docs.tests: Client-side vs server-side encryption when AWS must have access to neither the data nor the keys.
docs.expected: Client-side encryption (AWS Encryption SDK) with customer-controlled keys — only ciphertext reaches S3. Triggers: "encrypt before sending", "AWS never has access to plaintext or the keys".
docs.why_not: SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS are server-side: AWS encrypts and has access to the keys; Block Public Access is about exposure, not encryption.

question.stem: An application must encrypt data before sending it to S3 so that AWS never has access to plaintext or the keys. Which approach satisfies this requirement?
options: Client-side encryption using the AWS Encryption SDK with keys the client controls
question.explanation: Client-side encryption encrypts data before upload using keys the client controls, so AWS only ever stores ciphertext and never sees plaintext or the keys. SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS are server-side, meaning AWS performs the encryption and has access to the keys. Block Public Access controls accessibility, not encryption.

docs.concept: IAM: least privilege — Resource = ARN of a specific secret
docs.tests: How to restrict an app to a single secret in an IAM policy.
docs.expected: Action secretsmanager:GetSecretValue + Resource = ARN of the specific secret. Triggers: "specific secret but nothing else", "least privilege".
docs.why_not: Resource "*" grants access to all secrets; secretsmanager:* and AdministratorAccess are grossly excessive permissions.

question.stem: A team needs to allow an application to retrieve a specific secret but nothing else, following least privilege. Which IAM policy element best restricts this?
options: A policy with Resource set to the specific secret ARN for secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
A policy granting secretsmanager:* on all secrets
A policy with Resource set to * for secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
question.explanation: Scoping the Resource to the specific secret ARN and limiting the action to GetSecretValue enforces least privilege. A wildcard resource grants access to all secrets. The secretsmanager:* action and AdministratorAccess vastly exceed what the application requires.

docs.concept: EBS: encryption by default at the Region level
docs.tests: How to guarantee all new EBS volumes are encrypted without relying on users.
docs.expected: Enable EBS encryption by default in the EC2 settings of each Region — new volumes and snapshots are encrypted automatically. Triggers: "always encrypted", "without relying on users".
docs.why_not: Manual encryption after creation — errors and a plaintext window; an SCP denying RunInstances blocks all launches; S3 default encryption doesn't apply to EBS.

question.stem: A company wants to ensure that EBS volumes attached to new EC2 instances are always encrypted, organization-wide, without relying on users to select encryption. What should they do?
options: Enable EBS encryption by default in each region's EC2 settings
Use an SCP to deny RunInstances
Manually encrypt each volume after creation
question.explanation: Enabling EBS encryption by default per region automatically encrypts all new volumes and snapshots without user action. Manual post-creation encryption is error-prone and leaves a plaintext window. Denying RunInstances blocks all launches. S3 default encryption is unrelated to EBS.

docs.concept: IAM Identity Center: centralized workforce SSO across many accounts
docs.tests: Choosing a service to centrally manage employee access to multiple accounts with an external IdP.
docs.expected: AWS IAM Identity Center — SSO, external IdP integration, permission sets assigned to accounts. Triggers: "human users", "multiple AWS accounts", "single sign-on", "external identity provider".
docs.why_not: Cognito identity pools — for application end users; STS only issues credentials; IAM groups in each account — not centralized.

question.stem: An organization wants to centrally manage permissions for human users across multiple AWS accounts and integrate with an external identity provider for single sign-on. Which service is designed for this?
question.explanation: IAM Identity Center provides centralized workforce SSO across multiple accounts and integrates with external IdPs, assigning permission sets per account. Cognito identity pools target application end users. STS issues credentials but is not a management console for workforce access. Per-account IAM groups do not provide centralized cross-account SSO.

docs.concept: GuardDuty: threat detection (compromised credentials, malicious IPs)
docs.tests: Which managed service detects active threats: unusual API calls, communication with known malicious IPs.
docs.expected: Amazon GuardDuty — ML + threat intelligence over CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; enabled in one click. Triggers: "compromised credentials", "unusual API calls", "known malicious IPs", "minimal setup".
docs.why_not: Inspector — software vulnerabilities; Config — configuration compliance; Trusted Advisor — best-practice checks.

question.stem: A company suspects compromised credentials are being used to make unusual API calls and to communicate with known malicious IPs. Which managed service detects this threat with minimal setup?
question.explanation: GuardDuty continuously analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs using threat intelligence and ML to detect compromised credentials and malicious-IP communication with minimal setup. Config tracks configuration compliance. Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks. Inspector assesses software vulnerabilities, not active threats.

docs.concept: VPC endpoints: interface for AWS services + gateway for S3, no NAT
docs.tests: How to give private-subnet instances access to Systems Manager and S3 without internet or a NAT gateway.
docs.expected: Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for Systems Manager (ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages) + a gateway endpoint for S3. Triggers: "private subnet", "without traversing the public internet", "avoids a NAT gateway".
docs.why_not: An IGW or public IP exposes instances to the internet; a public proxy still goes over the internet.

question.stem: A workload running in a private subnet must access AWS Systems Manager and S3 without traversing the public internet. Which approach is MOST secure and avoids a NAT gateway?
options: Route traffic through a public proxy server
Attach an internet gateway to the private subnet
Use VPC interface endpoints for Systems Manager and a gateway endpoint for S3
Assign public IPs to the instances
question.explanation: Interface (PrivateLink) endpoints for Systems Manager and a gateway endpoint for S3 keep traffic on the AWS private network, avoiding both the internet and NAT charges. Attaching an internet gateway or assigning public IPs exposes instances. A public proxy still traverses the internet.

docs.concept: Inspector: vulnerability scanning for EC2 and container images
docs.tests: Which service automatically scans EC2 and container images for software vulnerabilities and network exposure.
docs.expected: Amazon Inspector — continuous scanning of EC2 and ECR images for CVEs and network reachability. Triggers: "software vulnerabilities", "container images", "unintended network exposure".
docs.why_not: Macie — sensitive data in S3; Shield — DDoS; WAF — web request filtering.

question.stem: A company needs to scan EC2 instances and container images for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure automatically. Which service should they enable?
question.explanation: Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2 instances and ECR container images for software vulnerabilities and network reachability issues. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. Shield protects against DDoS. WAF filters web requests; none of these perform vulnerability assessment.

docs.concept: KMS: key policy as the primary access control for a key
docs.tests: How to restrict a customer managed key to a single IAM role, controlled on the key itself.
docs.expected: A KMS key policy granting only that role kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt. Triggers: "usable only by a specific IAM role", "control this directly on the key".
docs.why_not: A bucket policy governs S3, not the key; a security group — network traffic; an SCP denying all KMS actions also blocks legitimate use.

question.stem: A company wants its KMS customer managed key to be usable only by a specific IAM role and wants to control this directly on the key. What should they configure?
options: A KMS key policy that grants the specific role kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt
An SCP denying all KMS actions
question.explanation: The KMS key policy is the primary access control for a key and can grant only the specified role the required actions. A bucket policy controls S3, not the key. Security groups govern network traffic. An SCP denying all KMS actions would block legitimate use too.

docs.concept: S3 Object Lock: compliance mode (WORM, not even root can delete)
docs.tests: How to guarantee nobody, including administrators, can delete or modify S3 logs during the retention period.
docs.expected: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode — WORM, retention can't be removed even by root. Triggers: "cannot be deleted or altered by anyone, including administrators", "fixed retention period", "regulated".
docs.why_not: Versioning allows deleting versions; an administrator can change a bucket policy; lifecycle expiration actually deletes objects. (Governance mode — privileged users can bypass it.)

question.stem: A regulated company must guarantee that audit logs in an S3 bucket cannot be deleted or altered by anyone, including administrators, for a fixed retention period. Which feature provides this?
options: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
question.explanation: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode enforces WORM retention that not even the root user can override during the retention period, satisfying strict immutability requirements. Versioning alone allows deletion of versions. Lifecycle rules expire objects. A bucket policy can be changed by an administrator, so it is not tamper-proof.

docs.concept: EKS: IRSA — IAM roles for pods via OIDC provider
docs.tests: Mechanism that gives individual EKS pods their own scoped AWS permissions.
docs.expected: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA): a service account is linked to an IAM role via the cluster's OIDC provider. Triggers: "pods get scoped AWS permissions", "service accounts".
docs.why_not: A shared node instance profile gives all pods the same broad permissions; access keys in Kubernetes secrets are long-lived; a NAT gateway has nothing to do with IAM.

question.stem: An application uses IAM roles for service accounts in Amazon EKS so that pods get scoped AWS permissions. Which mechanism enables this?
options: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) using an OIDC provider
Storing access keys in Kubernetes secrets
Node instance profile shared by all pods
question.explanation: IRSA associates a Kubernetes service account with an IAM role via the cluster's OIDC provider, giving individual pods least-privilege credentials. A shared node instance profile grants all pods the same broad permissions. Static access keys in secrets are long-lived and insecure. A NAT gateway is unrelated to IAM.

docs.concept: IAM conditions: aws:SourceIp and aws:SecureTransport
docs.tests: Which condition keys restrict requests to the corporate IP range and HTTPS.
docs.expected: aws:SourceIp = corporate CIDR + aws:SecureTransport = true. Triggers: "originates from corporate IP range", "over TLS".
docs.why_not: s3:x-amz-acl public-read exposes data; aws:PrincipalOrgID with a random value is meaningless; ec2:InstanceType is irrelevant here.

question.stem: A company wants to allow specific actions only when the request originates from their corporate IP range and over TLS. Which IAM/bucket policy conditions enforce this? (Choose two)
options: aws:SourceIp condition matching the corporate CIDR
question.explanation: The aws:SourceIp condition restricts requests to the corporate CIDR, and aws:SecureTransport set to true enforces HTTPS/TLS. The public-read ACL would expose data. PrincipalOrgID with a random value is meaningless, and ec2:InstanceType is irrelevant to these requirements.

docs.concept: HA: Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB
docs.tests: How to design a stateless web tier that survives the failure of an entire AZ.
docs.expected: Auto Scaling group across at least 2 AZs + ALB in the same AZs. Triggers: "entire Availability Zone fails", "stateless web tier", "MOST highly available".
docs.why_not: A single instance (even large or with an Elastic IP) or two in one AZ go down with the AZ.

question.stem: A stateless web tier behind an Application Load Balancer must remain available even if an entire Availability Zone fails. What is the MOST highly available design?
options: A single large EC2 instance in one AZ
A single instance with an Elastic IP
Two instances in the same AZ
An Auto Scaling group spanning at least two AZs with the ALB across the same AZs
question.explanation: An Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs combined with an ALB distributing to those AZs survives a full AZ failure by maintaining capacity elsewhere. A single instance or two instances in one AZ both fail when that AZ goes down. An Elastic IP does not provide multi-AZ resilience.

docs.concept: RDS Multi-AZ: synchronous standby and automatic failover
docs.tests: Multi-AZ vs read replicas for relational DB high availability.
docs.expected: RDS Multi-AZ — synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ, automatic failover. Triggers: "automatic failover", "standby in another AZ", "synchronous replication".
docs.why_not: Read replica — asynchronous, for read scaling; Single-AZ — no standby; MySQL on a single EC2 — no built-in HA.

question.stem: An application requires a relational database with automatic failover to a standby in another AZ and synchronous replication. Which configuration meets this?
options: Amazon RDS read replica in the same AZ
Self-managed MySQL on a single EC2 instance
question.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically on failure. Single-AZ has no standby. A read replica is asynchronous and intended for scaling reads, not automatic failover. Self-managed MySQL on one instance has no built-in HA.

docs.concept: DR strategies: Warm standby — scaled-down copy in another Region, RTO minutes
docs.tests: Choosing a DR strategy: recover in another Region within minutes with minimal data loss, without full duplication.
docs.expected: Warm standby: an always-running scaled-down copy in a second Region + continuous data replication; scales up during a disaster. Triggers: "within minutes", "minimal data loss", "avoid running full duplicate infrastructure".
docs.why_not: Backup and restore — hours; Pilot light — slow scale-up (compute is off); Single-Region multi-AZ doesn't protect against a Region failure; Multi-site — full duplicate, expensive.

question.stem: A company runs a critical workload and must recover in another AWS Region within minutes with minimal data loss, but wants to avoid running full duplicate infrastructure continuously. Which DR strategy fits BEST?
options: Warm standby with continuous data replication and scaled-down compute
question.explanation: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but always-running copy in another Region with continuous data replication, allowing recovery in minutes while avoiding the cost of full duplicate capacity. Backup and restore takes hours. Pilot light requires significant scale-up time. Single-Region multi-AZ does not protect against a Region failure.

docs.concept: DynamoDB global tables: multi-Region active-active replication
docs.tests: How to keep DynamoDB reads/writes working through a full Region outage with low latency for users in different Regions.
docs.expected: DynamoDB global tables — multi-Region active-active replication, local reads and writes. Triggers: "entire Region becomes unavailable", "reads and writes", "low-latency from multiple Regions".
docs.why_not: DAX — cache within a single Region; on-demand capacity — scales throughput but single Region; Streams + Lambda backup — not active-active.

question.stem: A DynamoDB table must remain available for reads and writes even if an entire Region becomes unavailable, with low-latency access from users in multiple Regions. What should be used?
options: DynamoDB with a single Region and DAX
DynamoDB on-demand capacity in one Region
DynamoDB Streams to a Lambda backup
question.explanation: DynamoDB global tables provide multi-Region, active-active replication, delivering local low-latency access and resilience to a Region outage. DAX is an in-Region cache. On-demand capacity scales throughput but stays single-Region. Streams plus Lambda backups do not provide active-active multi-Region availability.

docs.concept: SQS: buffer between web tier and workers + Auto Scaling on queue depth
docs.tests: How to absorb unpredictable load spikes and decouple order processing from the web tier.
docs.expected: SQS queue between the web tier and order processors + EC2 Auto Scaling on queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessages / backlog per instance). Triggers: "unpredictable spikes", "flash sales", "decouple order processing".
docs.why_not: A fixed fleet and synchronous processing in a single RDS can't handle bursts; keeping orders in instance memory means data loss.

question.stem: An ecommerce site experiences unpredictable traffic spikes during flash sales. The architecture must scale automatically and decouple order processing from the web tier. Which combination is MOST appropriate? (Choose two)
options: Place an Amazon SQS queue between the web tier and order processors
Store orders only in instance memory
Use EC2 Auto Scaling driven by queue depth for the processors
Send all orders directly to a fixed-size EC2 fleet
Use a single RDS instance to process orders synchronously
question.explanation: An SQS queue decouples the web tier from order processing, absorbing spikes, and Auto Scaling driven by queue depth (e.g., ApproximateNumberOfMessages) scales processors to demand. Synchronous RDS processing and a fixed fleet cannot absorb sudden spikes. Storing orders in instance memory risks data loss.

docs.concept: ElastiCache: cache frequent queries in front of RDS (read-heavy)
docs.tests: The most cost-effective way to cut RDS read latency when data is frequently re-read and slight staleness is acceptable.
docs.expected: Add ElastiCache in front of RDS to cache results of frequent queries. Triggers: "read-heavy", "frequently re-read", "tolerates slight staleness", "cost-effective".
docs.why_not: The largest instance class — expensive; moving to DynamoDB — a redesign; Multi-AZ improves availability, not read performance.

question.stem: A read-heavy application using Amazon RDS experiences high read latency during peak hours. The data is frequently re-read and tolerates slight staleness. What is the MOST cost-effective performance improvement?
options: Upgrade to the largest available instance class
Add an Amazon ElastiCache layer to cache frequent query results
question.explanation: ElastiCache offloads frequent reads from the database, reducing latency and load cost-effectively when staleness is acceptable. Upgrading to the largest instance is expensive and addresses scaling less efficiently. Switching to DynamoDB is a major rearchitecture. Multi-AZ improves availability, not read performance.

docs.concept: CloudFront: global delivery of static content from an S3 origin
docs.tests: How to give global users low latency and high availability for a static site and protect the origin from overload.
docs.expected: CloudFront with an S3 origin — caching at edge locations, offloading the origin. Triggers: "globally distributed users", "static website", "low latency", "protection against origin overload".
docs.why_not: Serving directly from S3 — no edge cache; a single EC2 — neither global nor HA; Route 53 latency routing to one server doesn't reduce latency.

question.stem: A globally distributed user base needs low-latency access to a static website with high availability and protection against origin overload. Which solution is BEST?
options: Use a single EC2 web server with an Elastic IP
Use Amazon CloudFront with an S3 origin
Serve directly from a single S3 bucket
Use Route 53 latency routing to one regional server
question.explanation: CloudFront caches content at global edge locations, lowering latency, increasing availability, and shielding the S3 origin from load. Serving directly from S3 lacks edge caching. A single EC2 server is neither global nor highly available. Route 53 latency routing to one server cannot reduce global latency to a single location.

docs.concept: SNS: pub/sub fan-out to SQS and Lambda
docs.tests: Which service implements pub/sub where one event is delivered to multiple independent subscribers.
docs.expected: Amazon SNS topic with SQS, Lambda, HTTP subscribers (fan-out). Triggers: "publish/subscribe", "fans out to multiple independent consumers".
docs.why_not: SQS alone — point-to-point; Step Functions — orchestration; Kinesis Data Streams — streaming data, not simple fan-out delivery.

question.stem: A company wants to decouple microservices using a publish/subscribe model where one event fans out to multiple independent consumers, including SQS queues and Lambda functions. Which service is designed for this?
question.explanation: Amazon SNS provides pub/sub fan-out, delivering each message to multiple subscribers such as SQS queues, Lambda, and HTTP endpoints. SQS alone is point-to-point. Step Functions orchestrates workflows. Kinesis is for streaming data, not simple fan-out notification.

docs.concept: Stateless: move session state to ElastiCache/DynamoDB
docs.tests: How to stop users being logged out on scale-in when sessions are stored in instance memory.
docs.expected: Store session state in ElastiCache or DynamoDB — the web tier becomes stateless. Triggers: "session state in instance memory", "logouts when instances scale in".
docs.why_not: Sticky sessions still lose state when an instance terminates; disabling Auto Scaling removes elasticity; a bigger instance doesn't fix the problem.

question.stem: An application stores session state in EC2 instance memory, causing user logouts when instances scale in. What change improves resilience with the LEAST disruption?
options: Store session state in Amazon ElastiCache or DynamoDB
question.explanation: Externalizing session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB makes the web tier stateless, so scaling in no longer logs users out. Disabling Auto Scaling removes elasticity. Sticky sessions still lose state when an instance terminates. Larger instances do not solve state loss.

docs.concept: Step Functions: orchestrate Lambda with branching, retries, error handling
docs.tests: Choosing a service for visual orchestration of multiple Lambdas with branching and retries.
docs.expected: AWS Step Functions — state machine with built-in Choice, Retry, Catch and visualization. Triggers: "coordinate multiple Lambda functions", "branching logic, retries, error handling", "visual".
docs.why_not: SQS and SNS — messaging, not orchestration; AWS Batch — batch computing without a state machine.

question.stem: A workflow must coordinate multiple Lambda functions with branching logic, retries, and error handling in a visual, maintainable way. Which service is BEST?
question.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with built-in branching, retries, and error handling, visualized as a state machine. SQS and SNS handle messaging, not orchestration. Batch runs batch compute jobs but lacks the visual state-machine orchestration.

docs.concept: EFS: shared NFS file system for many Linux EC2 across multiple AZs
docs.tests: Choosing storage accessible concurrently by hundreds of Linux instances across AZs with automatic scaling.
docs.expected: Amazon EFS — managed elastic NFS, multi-AZ, concurrent access. Triggers: "shared file storage", "concurrently from hundreds of Linux instances", "multiple AZs", "scaling automatically".
docs.why_not: EBS — attached to one instance (Multi-Attach only within one AZ); S3 — object storage, not POSIX; instance store — ephemeral and local.

question.stem: A company needs shared file storage accessible concurrently from hundreds of Linux EC2 instances across multiple AZs, scaling automatically. Which service fits?
options: Amazon S3 mounted as a block device
question.explanation: Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system accessible concurrently from many instances across AZs. EBS attaches to a single instance (except limited multi-attach in one AZ). S3 is object storage, not a POSIX file system. Instance store is ephemeral and local.

docs.concept: Global Accelerator: static anycast IPs and fast failover over AWS backbone
docs.tests: Choosing a service to route to the nearest healthy regional endpoint with static IPs.
docs.expected: AWS Global Accelerator — 2 static anycast IPs, traffic over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint, fast failover, TCP/UDP. Triggers: "static anycast IPs", "AWS global network", "fast failover", "closest healthy endpoint".
docs.why_not: CloudFront — caches HTTP(S) content, not arbitrary TCP/UDP endpoints; Route 53 weighted — by weight, not proximity; ALB — regional.

question.stem: A company wants to route users to the closest healthy regional endpoint and improve performance using the AWS global network, with static anycast IPs and fast failover. Which service should they use?
question.explanation: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs, routes traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint, and fails over quickly. CloudFront caches content but is for HTTP(S) delivery, not arbitrary TCP/UDP endpoints. Weighted routing distributes by weight, not proximity health. A single ALB is regional.

docs.concept: SQS FIFO: strict ordering and exactly-once processing
docs.tests: Which queue guarantees message ordering and exactly-once processing for financial transactions.
docs.expected: SQS FIFO queue — ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing (deduplication). Triggers: "strict ordering", "exactly-once", "financial transactions".
docs.why_not: SQS standard — at-least-once and best-effort ordering; SNS standard — no ordering guarantee; Firehose — delivery to storage, not transactional messaging.

question.stem: A messaging system requires strict ordering of messages and exactly-once processing for financial transactions. Which option meets this?
question.explanation: SQS FIFO queues guarantee ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group, ideal for financial transactions. Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. SNS standard topics do not guarantee ordering. Firehose is for delivery to data stores, not ordered transactional messaging.

docs.concept: Fargate: serverless containers without managing servers
docs.tests: Choosing compute for containers that scale to zero without managing instances.
docs.expected: AWS Fargate — serverless container execution (ECS/EKS), task count scales down to zero. Triggers: "containers", "scale to zero when idle", "without managing servers".
docs.why_not: ECS on EC2 and self-managed Kubernetes require managing servers; a fixed ASG doesn't scale to zero.

question.stem: A company runs a fleet of containers that must scale to zero when idle and start quickly on demand, without managing servers. Which compute option is MOST suitable?
options: A fixed EC2 Auto Scaling group
question.explanation: Fargate runs containers serverlessly, scaling task count up and down (including to zero) without managing instances. ECS on EC2 and self-managed Kubernetes require provisioning and managing servers. A fixed Auto Scaling group does not scale to zero cleanly and adds management overhead.

docs.concept: SQS: buffer requests when downstream is unavailable (loose coupling)
docs.tests: Which pattern keeps the system working while a dependency is temporarily unavailable.
docs.expected: An SQS queue buffers requests, processing is asynchronous — the consumer catches up after recovery. Triggers: "downstream dependency temporarily unavailable", "buffering requests", "loose coupling".
docs.why_not: Synchronous REST and direct TCP connections fail along with the dependency; a shared table with polling is fragile tight coupling.

question.stem: An application must continue functioning if a downstream dependency is temporarily unavailable, buffering requests until it recovers. Which pattern provides this loose coupling?
options: An SQS queue buffering requests for asynchronous processing
A shared database table polled by both services
question.explanation: An SQS queue decouples producers from consumers, buffering messages so the system tolerates a temporarily unavailable downstream service. Synchronous REST and direct TCP connections fail when the dependency is down. A shared polled table is fragile and tightly couples schema and availability.

docs.concept: Aurora Global Database: cross-Region DR with fast promotion
docs.tests: Which Aurora feature provides cross-Region DR with minimal RTO via a continuously updated replica.
docs.expected: Aurora Global Database (or a cross-Region read replica) — replication to another Region with ~1 s lag, fast promotion. Triggers: "another Region", "minimal RTO", "continuously updated read replica", "fast promotion".
docs.why_not: Automated snapshots — slow recovery; Multi-AZ doesn't protect against a Region failure; manual export to S3 — high RPO and slow recovery.

question.stem: A company wants minimal-RTO recovery for a database in another Region and is willing to keep a continuously updated read replica running. Which RDS feature supports cross-Region disaster recovery for Aurora with fast promotion?
options: Aurora cross-Region read replica or Global Database
question.explanation: Aurora Global Database (or a cross-Region replica) continuously replicates to another Region with low lag and supports fast promotion for DR. Snapshots only require lengthy restore. Multi-AZ does not protect against a Region failure. Manual S3 exports have high RPO and slow recovery.

docs.concept: ELB: NLB — Layer 4, millions of requests/s, preserves client IP
docs.tests: Choosing a load balancer type for very high TCP load with ultra-low latency and source IP preservation.
docs.expected: Network Load Balancer — Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS), millions of rps, ultra-low latency, preserves the client source IP. Triggers: "millions of requests per second", "TCP", "ultra-low latency", "preserves client source IP".
docs.why_not: ALB — Layer 7 for HTTP(S); Classic — legacy; Gateway Load Balancer — for inserting virtual appliances.

question.stem: A company needs a load balancer that handles millions of requests per second of TCP traffic with ultra-low latency and preserves the client source IP. Which load balancer is BEST?
question.explanation: The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, handles extremely high throughput with ultra-low latency, and can preserve the client source IP. The ALB is Layer 7 for HTTP(S). The Classic Load Balancer is legacy. The Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting virtual appliances, not general TCP load balancing.

docs.concept: Athena: serverless SQL over data in S3 (Parquet)
docs.tests: Choosing a service for ad hoc SQL queries on large Parquet files in S3 without managing servers.
docs.expected: Amazon Athena — serverless SQL directly over S3, pay per data scanned. Triggers: "ad hoc SQL", "Parquet in S3", "without managing servers".
docs.why_not: Redshift — a cluster for a persistent data warehouse; RDS — transactional DB; persistent EMR — operational overhead.

question.stem: An analytics team runs ad hoc SQL queries directly against large datasets stored as Parquet files in S3 without managing any servers. Which service is MOST appropriate?
question.explanation: Amazon Athena queries data in S3 using standard SQL with no infrastructure to manage and is ideal for ad hoc analysis of Parquet files. Redshift requires a provisioned (or serverless) cluster better suited to sustained warehousing. RDS is a transactional database. Persistent EMR clusters add operational overhead.

docs.concept: Kinesis Data Streams: real-time ingestion, multiple consumers and replay
docs.tests: Choosing a service for a clickstream with multiple independent consumers and the ability to re-read data.
docs.expected: Kinesis Data Streams — high-volume real-time, multiple independent consumers, records retained for replay within the retention period. Triggers: "real-time", "clickstream", "multiple independent consumers", "replay".
docs.why_not: SQS deletes messages after processing, point-to-point; SNS — pub/sub with no retention for replay; Glue — ETL, not real-time ingestion.

question.stem: A company ingests high-volume clickstream data in real time and needs to process it with multiple independent consumers, retaining records for replay. Which service fits BEST?
question.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams ingests high-volume real-time data, supports multiple consumers reading independently, and retains records for replay within the retention window. SQS deletes messages after consumption and is point-to-point. SNS is pub/sub without ordered replayable storage. Glue is ETL, not real-time ingestion.

docs.concept: DB migration: SCT for schema + DMS with CDC for heterogeneous migration
docs.tests: Which tools are needed to migrate Oracle → Aurora PostgreSQL with schema conversion and minimal downtime.
docs.expected: AWS SCT converts Oracle schema and code → PostgreSQL; AWS DMS moves the data with ongoing replication (CDC) until cutover. Triggers: "Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL", "converting the schema", "minimizing downtime".
docs.why_not: Snowball — offline shipping, doesn't convert engines or replicate; DataSync — files, not databases; Kinesis — not a schema migration tool.

question.stem: A company needs to migrate an on-premises Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL, converting the schema and minimizing downtime. Which combination should they use? (Choose two)
options: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) for continuous replication during cutover
AWS DataSync for the database engine conversion
AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert the schema
Amazon Kinesis to stream schema changes
AWS Snowball to ship the running database
question.explanation: SCT converts Oracle schema and code to PostgreSQL, while DMS performs the data migration with ongoing replication to minimize downtime at cutover. Snowball ships data offline but does not convert engines or replicate live. Kinesis and DataSync are not database schema or heterogeneous migration tools.

docs.concept: S3 Lifecycle: transition to Standard-IA for infrequent access with ms retrieval
docs.tests: Picking a storage class after 30 days of frequent access, when access becomes rare but must be millisecond-fast.
docs.expected: Lifecycle transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days — cheaper storage, millisecond retrieval. Triggers: "frequently for 30 days, then rarely", "retrievable within milliseconds", "cost-effective".
docs.why_not: Everything in Standard — more expensive; Glacier Deep Archive — hours to retrieve; One Zone-IA from day one — ignores the frequent access in the first 30 days and stores in a single AZ.

question.stem: An application's images stored in S3 are accessed frequently for 30 days, then rarely but must be retrievable within milliseconds when needed. What is the MOST cost-effective lifecycle configuration?
options: Transition to S3 One Zone-IA in a single AZ immediately
Transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days
Transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
question.explanation: S3 Standard-IA offers lower storage cost for infrequently accessed data while retaining millisecond retrieval, fitting the post-30-day pattern. Keeping everything in Standard costs more. Glacier Deep Archive has retrieval delays of hours. One Zone-IA reduces durability across AZs and applying it immediately ignores the frequent first 30 days.

docs.concept: Glue: serverless ETL, crawlers and Data Catalog
docs.tests: Which service provides serverless ETL that crawls, catalogs and transforms data in an S3 data lake.
docs.expected: AWS Glue — crawlers populate the Glue Data Catalog, ETL jobs transform the data. Triggers: "serverless ETL", "crawl, catalog, and transform", "data lake".
docs.why_not: Athena — queries, but no ETL/crawling; QuickSight — visualization; Lambda alone — no managed catalog or ETL framework.

question.stem: A data lake requires serverless ETL to crawl, catalog, and transform data in S3 for analytics. Which service provides this?
question.explanation: AWS Glue provides serverless ETL with crawlers that catalog data and jobs that transform it, integrating with the Glue Data Catalog.
